introResultSentence: The outcome is a negative result with a clear shape: in none of the three models does either signal add to the other (all primary contrasts within $\pm4$\pp{} except one \emph{negative} one), the stage-only arm is never significantly worse than the official checkpoint, and the arms that draw boxes during training carry every significant loss, up to $-10$ to $-11$\pp{} on the two world-action models.
abstractResultSentence: The pre-registered contrasts are null in all three models: given one signal, adding the other changes success by at most $+3.5$\pp{}, and for Awomo-0.5V adding the box channel costs $8.5$\pp{} ($p=0.03$). Against the official checkpoints, every adapted XR-1 arm gains $6.5$--$7.5$\pp{}, driven by the seen tasks, while both Awomo models lose up to $10$--$11$\pp{} in the arms that saw boxes during training. Stage supervision is the harmless signal; box supervision can backfire when the policy's world-model pathway consumes the painted frame.
conclusionSentence: We found no evidence that the two signals are complementary, a consistent small gain for XR-1 that we cannot attribute to either signal, and a consistent loss for the world-action models whenever boxes were drawn into their training frames. The practical lesson is asymmetric: a stage head is a cheap and harmless addition, whereas visual prompts that are present at training time and absent at test time are a liability for policies that predict future frames.
labelAuditText: Of the 103 camera views with a visible-target label, 93 (90\%) bound the described target (eight of them the whole appliance rather than the named part); the ten errors are six robot links, three wrong instances and one unrelated object (details in the supplement).
